title: Asteria Financial x Redwood Inference — Security review + incident communications
summary: Customer asked for clarity on Redwood’s public status page accuracy and granularity, incident update cadence, and whether Redwood provides post-incident summaries suitable for enterprise vendor risk. Redwood explained current practices and the in-flight “status page transparency upgrades” project: more granular components (Streaming, Embeddings, Rerank, Console, region-specific serving), standard phase-based update templates with next-update timestamps, and customer-facing post-incident summaries aligned to internal postmortems with redaction guidance (target within 3 business days for Sev1+). Security team discussed disclosure boundaries (no customer names, no exploit details), and how comms align with SOC 2 controls, audit logging, and support escalation paths.
topics: Public status page: components, what “degraded” means, region vs global impact
Incident comms cadence (investigating/identified/monitoring/resolved) and update SLAs
Customer-facing post-incident summaries: content, timeline, redaction/disclosure policy
Security/compliance: SOC 2, audit logs, encryption/KMS, SSO/SAML, data retention
Dedicated vs Hosted API: isolation expectations and comms during partial degradations
questions: Can the status page reflect partial impact (e.g., streaming-only errors) without marking the whole API down?
Do you publish a post-incident report, and what’s the expected timeframe?
How frequently do you update during a long-running incident (hourly vs ad hoc)?
Will you show region-specific issues (us-east vs eu-west) and model-family issues?
What do you consider sensitive and therefore not publishable in incident summaries?
action_items: Naomi Feldman (Redwood) - Send Asteria Financial a copy of Redwood incident communications overview + current status page explanation by 2024-07-12
Marcus Lin (Redwood) - Share SOC 2 report access instructions and security FAQ (SSO, encryption, logging) by 2024-07-12
Devon Price (Redwood) - Provide a sample customer-facing post-incident summary (sanitized) and template by 2024-07-16
Priya Nair (Asteria) - Confirm preferred comms channels for Sev1 incidents (status page + email distro) and escalation contacts by 2024-07-17
Jordan Kim (Asteria) - Send vendor risk questionnaire sections specifically about incident reporting and availability definitions by 2024-07-17
next_steps: Redwood to provide sanitized example post-incident summary + templates and confirm expected SLA for publication.
Asteria to follow up with vendor risk questionnaire and clarify any contractual requirements for notifications.
Schedule 30-min follow-up focused on Dedicated/VPC deployment comms expectations and routing/fallback guidance.
transcript:
Meeting header
- Title: Asteria Financial x Redwood Inference — Security review + incident communications
- Date: 2024-07-10
- Time: 17:00 UTC
- Duration: 55 minutes
- Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Naomi Feldman, Marcus Lin, Devon Price, Olga Petrov
- Asteria Financial: Priya Nair (Security Eng), Jordan Kim (VRM), Elena Ruiz (Platform Eng), Sam Hsu (Procurement)

Auto-summary (generated)
Asteria’s security team asked about incident transparency: status page granularity, update cadence, and post-incident summaries. Redwood described ongoing improvements: new components (Streaming, Embeddings, Rerank, Console, Dedicated control plane, Private/VPC control plane, region serving), standardized templates with a next-update timestamp, and customer-facing post-incident summaries aligned to internal postmortems while avoiding sensitive disclosures.


[00:00] Naomi Feldman: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for joining. I’m Naomi, I run the commercial side for this deal. With me is Marcus from security engineering, Devon from our tooling team—he works on incident automation—and Olga from compliance.

[00:16] Priya Nair: Hi, Priya here, security engineering. We’re mainly here to understand your incident comms and status page. We’ve had some bad experiences where a vendor says “API degraded” and it’s actually like one endpoint, or just streaming.

[00:33] Jordan Kim: Jordan from vendor risk. Yeah and we also need to understand whether you provide post-incident reports, and how quickly.

[00:40] Elena Ruiz: Elena, platform engineering. I’ll probably ask a few operational questions—regions, failover, how we should interpret the status page.

[00:48] Sam Hsu: Sam, procurement. I’ll mostly listen; if there are commitments, we’ll capture those.

[00:54] Naomi Feldman: Perfect. Maybe to level-set: you’re evaluating Redwood for LLM inference, likely Dedicated or Private, right?

[01:02] Elena Ruiz: We’re leaning Dedicated first. Possibly VPC down the line. We run a bunch of customer workflows that are latency sensitive and, uh, regulated-ish.

[01:12] Naomi Feldman: Got it. Marcus, do you want to lead with what we publish today and where we’re headed? Then we can go Q&A.

[01:19] Marcus Lin: Sure. So today we do have a public status page with major components. Historically it was a little too coarse, like “API” and “Console.” We’ve been improving that and we have an active project to increase granularity and standardize the incident updates.

[01:36] Priya Nair: Can you be specific on “granularity”? Like what will I see?

[01:41] Marcus Lin: Yeah. The planned components are things that map to what customers actually integrate with: API Gateway / Requesting, Streaming responses, Embeddings, Rerank, Console, then control plane components for Dedicated and Private deployments. And region-specific serving—so rather than “API Degraded,” you might see “Hosted API Serving - us-east degraded” or “Streaming degraded” depending on what’s affected.

[02:06] Elena Ruiz: That’s basically what we want. Because if it’s only streaming, we can toggle off streaming for a while. But if it’s all tokens, then we fail over.

[02:15] Devon Price: Yeah, and we’re also updating how we post. So it’s not just a generic “Investigating.” It’ll include: what’s impacted, mitigations/workarounds if we know them, and the next update time. Like “next update in 30 minutes” or “by 18:00 UTC.”

[02:32] Jordan Kim: So you’ll commit to that cadence? Like in the contract?

[02:37] Naomi Feldman: Contract language is a separate conversation, but we can talk about our standard practice and what we can commit to for enterprise. For this call, maybe we describe the operational SLA we target.

[02:47] Olga Petrov: From compliance, we typically define internal expectations and then we can align contractual notifications based on severity and customer tier. But we don’t want to over-promise what we can’t consistently meet.

[03:00] Priya Nair: Okay. Let’s break this down. First: status page accuracy. When do you post? Like do you wait until confirmed or do you post “investigating” quickly?

[03:10] Devon Price: The goal is time-to-first-update is quick. Like we don’t want to wait for root cause. We post “investigating” once we have strong indicators of customer impact. And the upgrade here is mapping internal alerting to public components, so the person on-call isn’t guessing.

[03:29] Elena Ruiz: That’s a huge one. I’ve seen on-calls mark the wrong thing because the taxonomy is confusing.

[03:35] Devon Price: Exactly. We’re implementing guided prompts in our incident bot—like a checklist. It asks: which components, which regions, what’s the observed impact, what’s the workaround, and it won’t let you publish an empty update.

[03:52] Priya Nair: So right now, what are the components? Is it too broad today?

[03:57] Naomi Feldman: Today it’s broader. Think “API,” “Console,” “Dedicated,” “Private,” with some regional notes. But we’ve had feedback exactly like you’re describing—streaming-only issues being labeled “API degraded,” which creates noise and support tickets.

[04:14] Jordan Kim: Do you have examples?

[04:17] Marcus Lin: We do have internal examples and we can provide a sanitized one. Like a case where streaming keep-alive timeouts caused disconnects. The underlying token generation was healthy but the stream transport was flaky.

[04:32] Elena Ruiz: That’s precisely the scenario.

[04:35] Priya Nair: Okay. Second topic: incident cadence. What do you do during a Sev1? Like every 30 minutes? Hourly?

[04:44] Marcus Lin: We’re standardizing it by severity. Generally: initial update quickly, then updates at a defined cadence, and each update includes “next update by X time.” For high severity we target 30 minutes; for lower severity, it might be 60 minutes or when there’s material change.

[05:02] Priya Nair: How do you define severity? Internal severity might not match customer impact.

[05:07] Devon Price: True. We’re adding a customer impact classifier helper so the language is consistent: “degraded performance,” “partial outage,” “elevated errors,” “increased latency.” And we map that to what customers see. It’s driven by SLO burn and actual error rates.

[05:25] Elena Ruiz: Are you going to show percent impact? Like 10% of requests fail?

[05:30] Marcus Lin: We generally avoid exact numbers publicly unless we’re confident they’re stable and not misleading. But we do aim to be specific: “some customers,” “a subset,” “requests in us-east,” “streaming only,” things like that.

[05:46] Priya Nair: That’s fine. We don’t need precise. We need actionable.

[05:51] Jordan Kim: Third: post-incident summaries. Do you publish them? Some vendors refuse.

[05:56] Naomi Feldman: We’re implementing consistent customer-facing post-incident summaries. The intent is to align with our internal postmortem, but redact sensitive bits. Target SLA is within 3 business days for Sev1 and up.

[06:12] Jordan Kim: “Target” vs “guarantee” is important. For our VRM, we at least need something within a week, usually.

[06:19] Olga Petrov: Right. We can define that for your enterprise contract as a commitment if needed, but we’re being careful because sometimes the internal postmortem takes longer when we’re coordinating with a cloud provider. But we can still publish a summary with known facts and update it later.

[06:39] Priya Nair: What’s in the summary? Timeline, root cause, prevention?

[06:44] Marcus Lin: Typically: impact, start/end times, affected components/regions, what caused it in a root cause category sense, what we did to mitigate, and what we’re changing to prevent recurrence. We avoid anything that’s vulnerability-like, and we don’t include customer names or specifics about a single customer’s traffic patterns.

[07:08] Elena Ruiz: Can you say “cloud provider outage”?

[07:11] Marcus Lin: Yes, we can say “upstream provider networking issue” or “cloud region networking degradation” depending. Sometimes we can’t name the provider if there are contractual constraints, but we can describe it in a customer-safe way.

[07:25] Priya Nair: That’s fine, we don’t need you to name them. We need to know if it’s inside your control plane, your runtime, or upstream.

[07:33] Devon Price: The summary includes a root cause category so it’s more than “we had an issue.” Like “capacity and routing,” “streaming transport,” “control plane configuration,” “upstream dependency.”

[07:46] Jordan Kim: And those summaries are public?

[07:48] Naomi Feldman: Our plan is: for major incidents, public summary on the status page; for enterprise customers, we can also email the summary or attach it to a ticket. If it’s Dedicated or Private, there might be account-specific comms as well.

[08:08] Sam Hsu: Just to check—if it’s Dedicated, do you still put it on a public page? Or is it private because it’s isolated?

[08:16] Marcus Lin: Good question. We typically publish service-level issues that affect multiple customers or the shared control plane. For a Dedicated single-tenant issue, we may post “Dedicated - degraded” if it’s systemic; if it’s isolated to one tenant, we usually communicate directly with that customer rather than broadcasting. That’s part of our disclosure policy.

[08:39] Priya Nair: That makes sense. But we still want transparency. Like if it’s your control plane in general, we want to see it.

[08:45] Marcus Lin: Yes.

[08:47] Elena Ruiz: On the status page, will you show “Dedicated control plane” separate from “Dedicated serving”? Because control plane down might mean we can’t scale, but serving might be okay.

[08:57] Devon Price: That’s exactly one of the components we’re adding. Control plane is separate from serving.

[09:03] Priya Nair: Okay. What about Private/VPC deployments? If we deploy in our VPC, do we still get status page updates?

[09:10] Naomi Feldman: Yes, you still get incident communications. The public page might show “Private control plane” if it’s a shared component; for VPC-specific, you’d get direct communications. And we can provide a private status channel if needed.

[09:26] Jordan Kim: So there’s a distinction: public status vs direct customer notification.

[09:30] Olga Petrov: Correct.

[09:32] Priya Nair: Another angle: Do you have “investigating, identified, monitoring, resolved” as your statuses? Some vendors misuse “identified.”

[09:42] Devon Price: Yes, and we’re standardizing the language so “identified” only when we have a high-confidence cause and we’re actively mitigating. “Monitoring” is after fix or mitigation is in place and we’re watching metrics for stability.

[09:56] Elena Ruiz: Please don’t say “resolved” when it’s actually “we put a band-aid and will do a real fix later.”

[10:03] Marcus Lin: Agree. In the resolution note, we’ll be explicit: “Mitigation applied, permanent fix scheduled,” if that’s the case. And the post-incident summary would capture follow-up work.

[10:18] Priya Nair: Can you talk about who approves comms? Like could an engineer post something sensitive?

[10:24] Marcus Lin: There’s a policy. For normal incidents, the incident commander or SRE lead can post status updates using templates. For anything that touches security, privacy, or legal constraints, we involve security/compliance reviewers before publishing a detailed summary.

[10:42] Jordan Kim: So security is in the loop.

[10:44] Marcus Lin: Yes.

[10:45] Naomi Feldman: We can share the high-level policy without internal names. But it’s basically: who can publish, what must never be disclosed, and when to consult.

[10:56] Priya Nair: Good. Now, status page “granularity” again. Will you have regional breakdown? Like us-east, us-west, eu-west.

[11:04] Devon Price: Yes, for hosted serving we’re adding region-level components. There’s also guidance on when to mark regional vs global. Sometimes a global issue is actually a region issue that’s causing failover pressure elsewhere.

[11:22] Elena Ruiz: That’s… yeah, cascade effects. We need to know where to route.

[11:27] Priya Nair: If you show a region is degraded, would you also publish customer guidance like “pin to another region” or “use fallback model”?

[11:35] Devon Price: In the template we include “customer actions” when it’s safe: retry with exponential backoff, temporarily disable streaming, choose fallback model family, avoid large max_tokens, or pin to a different region if you have that enabled.

[11:55] Naomi Feldman: And we’re careful not to push customers into unsafe behavior, like “turn off auth” or something. It’s mostly operational guidance.

[12:03] Jordan Kim: How do you handle data in status updates? Do you ever include request IDs, or customer identifiers?

[12:10] Marcus Lin: No customer names. We might include anonymized aggregates. For account-specific debugging, we use support channels and secure ticketing, not public status.

[12:24] Priya Nair: Okay.

[12:26] Elena Ruiz: Slight tangent: Do you have audit logs? Like for console actions.

[12:31] Marcus Lin: Yes. For enterprise tiers we provide audit logs for console and administrative actions. That’s separate from incident comms but often part of the same control environment.

[12:44] Olga Petrov: And we’re SOC 2 Type II. We can provide the report under NDA via our portal.

[12:51] Jordan Kim: Good. We’ll request that.

[12:54] Naomi Feldman: Coming back to comms: what’s your required cadence for Sev1? Just so we know.

[13:01] Priya Nair: Ideally first notice within 15 minutes if it’s customer impacting. Then updates every 30 minutes until there’s mitigation, then hourly.

[13:12] Naomi Feldman: That aligns with our target approach. I’m not going to promise 15 minutes on every case, but we are measuring time-to-first-update as a KPI.

[13:23] Devon Price: The automation helps. When an incident is opened, we auto-draft an “investigating” update with placeholders, so the on-call just fills in what’s known and hits publish after review.

[13:37] Elena Ruiz: Is that live already?

[13:39] Devon Price: It’s being rolled out with feature flags. Some parts are in pilot.

[13:46] Priya Nair: So you’re in transition.

[13:48] Naomi Feldman: Yes. The direction is clear; we’re implementing it now.

[13:54] Jordan Kim: What about post-incident summary timing—3 business days. Is that for all Sev1?

[14:01] Marcus Lin: That’s the internal SLA target for Sev1 and Sev0. For Sev2, it may be best-effort or included when requested.

[14:12] Priya Nair: What’s Sev0 vs Sev1 for you?

[14:15] Marcus Lin: Sev0 is broad outage or major data/security event. Sev1 is significant customer impact, partial outage, sustained elevated errors/latency. The exact rubric we can share at a high level.

[14:30] Elena Ruiz: If it’s an upstream provider issue that lasts two hours, is that a Sev1? Even though it’s not your bug.

[14:36] Marcus Lin: It can be, yes, if it impacts customers materially.

[14:41] Priya Nair: Do you include “root cause” if it’s provider?

[14:45] Marcus Lin: We include root cause category and a factual description. Sometimes the detailed root cause is “upstream provider networking disruption,” plus what we did—e.g., routing changes, capacity rebalance, resilience improvements.

[15:02] Devon Price: And we’ll be explicit about what we’re doing to prevent the same blast radius, even if the provider is the trigger.

[15:10] Jordan Kim: That’s what we care about.

[15:13] Naomi Feldman: Can I ask—have you had a bad experience with status pages not matching reality?

[15:18] Priya Nair: Yes. Another vendor said “all good” but only certain models were returning 5xx. They never said which model family was impacted, so we couldn’t switch.

[15:31] Devon Price: We’re considering model-family incidents as well. We might say “Model family X degraded,” or more commonly, “Rerank endpoint degraded,” depending on how customers think. We’re trying to keep it customer-comprehensible.

[15:47] Elena Ruiz: Please don’t expose internal service names like “scheduler.”

[15:50] Devon Price: Yeah. Internally it’s “scheduler” but externally we’ll probably call it “Capacity & Routing.”

[15:56] Priya Nair: That’s good.

[16:00] Jordan Kim: Another question: Do you ever backfill status incidents? Like if it was missed, do you post after the fact?

[16:07] Marcus Lin: If we missed a public update for a customer-impacting event, we try to correct and publish a summary and explain. One goal of the project is to reduce those misses.

[16:20] Priya Nair: Okay.

[16:22] Elena Ruiz: For Dedicated, do we have a separate private status page?

[16:26] Naomi Feldman: We can discuss options. Typically customers use the public page plus direct comms. Some customers request a private page or webhook integration; we can explore.

[16:38] Sam Hsu: If it’s a paid add-on, we’d want it in the order form.

[16:41] Naomi Feldman: Understood.

[16:44] Priya Nair: What about support escalation during an incident? Do you have a dedicated channel?

[16:50] Naomi Feldman: For enterprise, yes: a support SLA and escalation path. During an incident, we’ll post public updates and also coordinate via the support ticket or a designated email distro.

[17:03] Jordan Kim: Ok.

[17:05] Marcus Lin: Let me also mention disclosure constraints, because it’s important: we won’t publish exploit details, vulnerability-like info, or any individual customer impact. We do publish what’s necessary to understand risk and operational impact.

[17:22] Priya Nair: That’s aligned with our expectations.

[17:25] Elena Ruiz: Can we see a draft of the post-incident template?

[17:28] Devon Price: Yes. I can send a sanitized template with sections and example language.

[17:33] Naomi Feldman: We’ll send that as a follow-up.

[17:36] Jordan Kim: Another vendor asked us to rely on internal tickets rather than status page. For us, the status page is a trust signal. How do you ensure it matches internal incident state?

[17:47] Devon Price: That’s one of the automation items. We sync incident state transitions to a draft status update. It doesn’t auto-publish without human review, but it keeps them aligned and prompts the on-call when updates are overdue.

[18:04] Priya Nair: Good. Because otherwise it’s always stale.

[18:08] Naomi Feldman: Quick check—are you expecting “post-incident” summary for every blip, or just major ones?

[18:14] Jordan Kim: Major ones. Anything that violates SLA or is Sev1. But we might request one if there’s an unusual event.

[18:23] Olga Petrov: That’s consistent.

[18:26] Elena Ruiz: Technical question: if streaming fails, are non-streaming calls affected? Or can we just switch to non-streaming mode?

[18:34] Devon Price: Generally you can switch. There are cases where the underlying generation is fine but the stream transport is failing. That’s why separating streaming as a component matters.

[18:47] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[18:49] Priya Nair: Another security angle: do you provide incident notification via email to a security distro? Some vendors only do status page.

[18:56] Naomi Feldman: Yes, for enterprise we can configure a distro list for incident notifications. We just need contacts and severity thresholds.

[19:07] Sam Hsu: If that’s a contractual requirement, we should document it.

[19:11] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[19:13] Jordan Kim: Can you speak to your retention of incident artifacts? Like logs.

[19:18] Marcus Lin: We have defined log retention and access controls; customer data handling depends on deployment mode. For Hosted API, we minimize retention of payload content; operational logs and metrics are retained for reliability and security purposes. We can provide specifics in the security package.

[19:38] Priya Nair: Okay. And encryption at rest, KMS?

[19:42] Marcus Lin: Yes, encryption at rest and in transit. For private deployments, we can integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM depending on setup.

[19:52] Elena Ruiz: Back to the status page—will it include model catalog availability? Like “model A” down.

[19:58] Devon Price: We’re still deciding the customer-friendly layer. We might not list each model name as a component because it becomes noisy. But we can reference “model family” or “endpoint type,” and in the update text we can call out affected models if it’s clear and helpful.

[20:18] Priya Nair: Yeah, don’t make it 100 components. But enough to route.

[20:23] Naomi Feldman: Exactly.

[20:26] Jordan Kim: How do you handle “partial outage” definition? Like 5% errors—do you mark it degraded?

[20:33] Marcus Lin: It depends on duration and customer impact. We have internal thresholds tied to SLO burn. If it’s transient and self-heals, we may not post. If it’s sustained or impacting customers, we post “degraded performance” even if it’s not 100% down.

[20:52] Priya Nair: That’s reasonable.

[20:54] Elena Ruiz: Do you support webhooks from status page? We can integrate into our NOC.

[20:59] Naomi Feldman: Our status provider supports subscriptions and webhooks; we can confirm details. Devon, do we have that available?

[21:06] Devon Price: Yes. Most customers use email/RSS, but webhooks are possible. We can share a doc.

[21:14] Priya Nair: Nice.

[21:16] Jordan Kim: Let’s talk about commitments: you said “3 business days” for post-incident summary. Is that for the initial summary or final, including prevention items?

[21:27] Marcus Lin: Initial summary within that window, including what we know: impact, timeline, high-level cause, mitigations. If some prevention items are still being finalized, we can note them as “planned” and update later.

[21:44] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[21:46] Priya Nair: And cadence: “next update by X time.” That’s strong. Can you show “next update” on the status page?

[21:54] Devon Price: It’s in the update text, and we’re enforcing that the on-call includes it. Some status providers also allow custom fields, but we’re not relying on it. The key is consistent text.

[22:11] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[22:13] Naomi Feldman: Anything else on incident comms before we pivot to general security items?

[22:18] Priya Nair: One more: who writes the post-incident summary? SRE or comms?

[22:23] Marcus Lin: Typically the incident owner / incident commander, reviewed by SRE lead, and for sensitive incidents reviewed by security/compliance.

[22:33] Priya Nair: Okay.

[22:35] Jordan Kim: We will need the SOC2, pen test attestation, and your incident response policy excerpt.

[22:43] Olga Petrov: We can provide SOC 2 via our trust portal. Pen test summary we can share at a high level. IR policy excerpt—yes.

[22:54] Elena Ruiz: Also SSO/SAML for console.

[22:57] Marcus Lin: Yes, SSO/SAML and RBAC.

[23:01] Naomi Feldman: Cool. Maybe we keep this call focused; we can do a separate deep dive if needed. For today, the key was comms and transparency.

[23:11] Priya Nair: For me, the main takeaway is you’re improving the status page to show streaming vs embeddings vs rerank, plus region. That’s good.

[23:22] Devon Price: Yep.

[23:23] Jordan Kim: One last question—do you ever publish customer-impact classification like “some customers can’t access console but API is fine”?

[23:33] Marcus Lin: Yes, that’s the idea. Component-level, plus text describing what’s working and what isn’t.

[23:42] Priya Nair: Perfect.

[23:45] Naomi Feldman: Alright, let’s do recap and next steps. We’ll send: (1) the incident comms overview and status page “how to read it,” (2) a sanitized example post-incident summary plus template, (3) trust portal access instructions. And you’ll send the VRM questionnaire sections relevant to incident notifications.

[24:06] Jordan Kim: Yes.

[24:07] Priya Nair: Works.

[24:09] Elena Ruiz: Can we schedule a quick follow-up to talk about Dedicated comms specifically? Like what is public vs direct.

[24:16] Naomi Feldman: Yes. I’ll coordinate.

[24:18] Sam Hsu: And if you can put any comms commitments in writing, even non-contractually, that helps.

[24:23] Naomi Feldman: We can provide our standard expectations and then we can discuss contract terms later.

[24:30] Marcus Lin: Thanks all.

[24:32] Priya Nair: Thanks.

[24:33] Jordan Kim: Thank you.

[24:35] (crosstalk)

[24:38] Fireflies.ai: Meeting ended.

Note: Recording ended at ~24 minutes due to participant leaving the calendar early; remaining discussion continued offline in chat/email according to organizer notes. (Fireflies capture incomplete.)
